card.keepWhy: Even Shiva held out his bowl, and said thanks.
sources: The Annapurna legend of Varanasi (Kashi): Shiva calls the world, food included, an illusion; Parvati vanishes and food disappears; she appears in Kashi as Annapurna and feeds Shiva, who comes with a begging bowl (the film’s note: a well-loved legend of Varanasi)
The Annapurna temple in Varanasi, near the Kashi Vishwanath temple
Annapurna Stotram, attributed to Adi Shankara (“annapurne sadapurne…”), recited by many before meals
check: The legend’s textual source: it is a popular Varanasi telling; confirm “a legend of Varanasi” as the source line, and whether any Purana tells it this way.
Is Shiva calling food “maya” (illusion) the usual telling? The film says “food is just an illusion.”

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? how did your last meal go? did you notice it?
options: you’re not alone. listen to this one.
then ten seconds will help. listen.

steps.line: In a story told in the holy city of Varanasi, Shiva once said to Parvati: food is just an illusion. It doesn’t really matter.

steps.q: Shiva says food is only an illusion. What do you guess Parvati does?
o: Cooks him a feast to prove him wrong
Leaves for her father’s mountain home
steps.why: She vanishes, and as Shakti, the power that makes things grow, she takes every grain with her. Adi Shankara’s hymn to Annapurna ends each verse like a beggar: bhiksham dehi, give me alms.

steps.line: Parvati didn’t argue. She simply disappeared. And with her, all the food in the world vanished.
Gods, people and animals went hungry. Even Shiva.

steps.q: Shiva is the great yogi who sits on a mountain needing nothing. Why is it striking that he goes hungry?
o: The god who needs nothing finds out he needs food
He had fasted so long he forgot how to eat
He missed Parvati’s company, not her cooking
steps.why: The story turns his own words on him. Without the goddess, even the greatest renouncer has to eat.

steps.line: Then Parvati appeared in Varanasi as Annapurna, the goddess of food, and opened a kitchen.
steps.label: Annapurna

steps.q: Varanasi is Shiva’s own city. Where does Annapurna’s temple stand there today?
o: On the far bank of the Ganges, apart from him
High up the river, at the city’s edge
A short walk from the great Shiva temple
steps.why: The Annapurna temple sits near Kashi Vishwanath. Many in Varanasi say no one in the city goes hungry, because she feeds it.

steps.line: Shiva himself came with a begging bowl. She filled it, and he understood.
steps.label: Annapurna

steps.q: Why does the story bring Shiva to her kitchen as a beggar, and not as a god demanding food?
o: Beggars were always fed first in Varanasi
To be fed, even a god holds out his hands
He was hiding so she wouldn’t turn him away
steps.why: Paintings of this scene show Annapurna ladling food into Shiva’s bowl. Food is received as a gift, never just taken.

steps.line: Food is a gift worth noticing. Many Hindus still pause before eating, to offer it, and say thanks.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. the great god of the story stood with an empty bowl, and understood.
many hindus see food as a gift of the goddess, never just fuel. that’s why so many pause before eating, to offer the food and give thanks.

steps.q: Shiva said food was just an illusion. What does the story answer him?
o: He was right, but bodies still need feeding
Only food offered in a temple counts as holy
Ordinary food is sacred: it’s the goddess’s gift
steps.why: That’s why many Hindus offer a meal before eating it. Her name says it plainly: anna, food; purna, full.

today.say: before your next meal, put the phone down for ten seconds and say thanks: to god, the farmer, whoever cooked. many hindus offer the food first, and some say a short prayer to annapurna. you can say one, or just a quiet thank you. it’s your choice.
options: good. ten seconds, the way shiva held out his bowl.
then put something small by your plate as a reminder.
